Most of the plant species discussed in Subsection 2.2.3.1 would be adversely affected by the construction, operation, and maintenance of this alternative site. The Highlands Biological Station, Inc. (Bruce and Pittillo, 1974) identified the lower Thompson River Gorge (about 2 miles upstream from Lake Jocassee) as a very important bryophyte They identified such important tropical types as Isopterygium tenerum (rare), Leucodon julaceus, Leucobryum albidum, Entodon macropodus, Anomodon attenuatus, A. minor, Haplohymenius triste, and Brachythecium rotaeanum (not common). They recommend leaving the strip of steep-walled gorge with the old-growth trees intact to maintain the proper moist habitat. This would mean a strip about 1/4 mile wide (1/8 mile on each side of the river) be left in standing timber. The upper reservoir for this alternative site would inundate this area.
8.3.1.2 Fauna
Detailed data are not available on the current status of the fish and wildlife resources at the Long Spur Ridge site. The wildlife habitat and wildlife composition of the Long Spur Ridge site is expected to be similar to that described in Subsection 2.2.2 for the Bad Creek site. The 3-mile stretch of the Thompson River from the Highway 1149 bridge in Transylvania County to the South Carolina State line, which includes the Long Spur Ridge site, has an average width of 15 feet and covers 5 acres of stream area. This reach of the Thompson River is designated as native trout water and classified by the State of North Carolina as rainbow trout water, characterized by heavy, fast flows, and containing rainbow trout, dace, and chubs (Fish, 1968).
Development of the Long Spur Ridge site would create a reservoir with a surface area of 280 acres which would inundate land presently managed to some unknown extent for wildlife by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. Data regarding wildlife species inhabiting the Long Spur Ridge area are unavailable, but impacts similar in type to those for the Bad Creek area (see Subsections 3.1.2 and 3.2.2) would be expected.
Impoundment of the reservoir site would inundate about 3.4 miles of stream and would eliminate fish and other faunal species unable to adapt to reservoir conditions. Fishing would be precluded in the portion of the Thompson River and its tributaries to be inundated. Hunting use within the proposed reservoir site would also be lost.
